conceptTag: Is this app at product-market fit?
readerTitle: 4,000 downloads and a rave review: is this app at fit?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소매점용 재고 주문 앱, 물류용 배송 확인 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 앱의 핏은 얼마나 많이 들어왔는지가 아니라, 들어온 고객이 쓰기를 멈추지 않는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 다운로드, 언론 보도, 높은 설문 점수, 큰 고객사의 시범 계약이 있으면 제품-시장 적합성을 찾은 것이다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: CUS-03-03 (리텐션이 진짜 신호), CUS-03-06 (가짜 핏 신호)
모든 앱, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 3월 가입 매장 코호트: 1주차 100%, 4주차 45%, 8주차 22%, 12주차 10%. '10곳 중 1곳' 문구가 12주차 10%와 일치하는지 확인했습니다.
비교용 '평평해지는 곡선'(100%, 55%, 42%, 40%)은 실제 앱 데이터가 아니라 모양을 보여주기 위한 가상 곡선입니다. 카드에 'shape only'로 표시했습니다.
4,000 다운로드 중 12주차에 남은 비율을 따로 언급하지 않았습니다. 다운로드 수와 가입 매장 수를 같은 것으로 쓰지 않도록 문구를 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: 4,000 downloads and a rave review: is this app at fit?
body: Maya built an app that lets small corner shops reorder stock from wholesalers in a few taps.

In one month after a trade show: 4,000 downloads, a feature in a retail magazine, and a 4.6 out of 5 survey score. She is ready to hire three salespeople. First, let's check what those numbers really say.

image.label: A shop owner holding a phone beside half-empty shelves
image.brief: 동네 편의점 계산대 뒤에서 주인이 휴대폰으로 주문 앱을 보는 장면. 뒤 선반은 반쯤 비어 있음. 휴대폰 화면 옆에 '4,000 downloads', '4.6★' 말풍선이 떠 있음. 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which number tells Maya the most?
body: She can only track one number closely for the next month. Which one best shows whether shops truly need the app?

options.feedback: Downloads measure how many people heard about the app, not how many needed it. This is a classic **false sign of fit**: a launch spike can come from one trade show.
It shows people like the idea. But shops that quietly stopped using the app rarely answer surveys, so the score leans toward fans.

options.text: The share of shops still ordering through the app eight weeks after joining
options.feedback: This is **retention as the real signal**. It counts what shops do when no one is watching, which is the closest thing to proof of need.

cards.title: The line keeps falling.
body: Maya tracked every shop that joined in March. By week 12, only 1 in 10 still placed orders through the app. The curve never levels off.
The second line shows the shape fit tends to have: a drop at first, then a flat line of customers who stay.

cards.title: Look for the line that stops falling.
body: Some customers always leave early. That is normal. What matters is whether the curve **flattens**: a group that keeps coming back week after week.
A flat line means the app does a job someone can't easily do without it. A line sliding toward zero means each new shop is just passing through, however many arrive.

image.label: Two retention curves, one sliding to zero, one flattening
image.brief: 그래프 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽은 0을 향해 계속 떨어지는 곡선(라벨 'Passing through'), 오른쪽은 처음엔 떨어지다 평평해지는 곡선(라벨 'Staying'). 평평한 부분을 밝은 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Attention is not need.
body: Maya's three proud numbers all measure interest. The trade show brought curious owners. The magazine brought more. The survey reached the happiest ones.

**False signs of fit** feel like progress because they are real numbers that go up. But none of them answers the only question that matters: did shops change how they reorder stock, and keep doing it?

cards.title: Should Maya hire the salespeople?
body: She has the budget for three hires. Retention is sliding toward zero. What's the wiser next step?

options.text: Hire them now to keep the momentum going
options.feedback: More sales would pour more shops into a curve that empties out. The false signs would grow while retention stays the same.

options.text: Hold off, and call the shops still ordering in week 12 to learn why they stayed
options.feedback: The 10% who stayed hold the clue to real need. **Retention** tells Maya where to look before she spends on growth.

options.text: Hold off, and build the five features the survey asked for
options.feedback: Waiting is right, but survey wish lists come mostly from people who answer surveys. The shops that left may need something else entirely.

cards.title: Measure at the right rhythm.
body: Retention only means something if you measure it at the pace customers naturally buy. A shop reorders weekly, so weekly use is fair. An app for yearly tax filing would look broken on the same chart.
Small early groups are also noisy. Twenty shops leaving can be one bad month.
The same test works off-screen too. A wholesaler launching a new product line should watch reorders, not the first big order.

cards.title: Now it's a delivery app for trucking firms.
body: Leo's app lets drivers record proof of delivery with a photo and signature. Which is the strongest sign of fit?

options.text: A large distributor signed a paid six-month pilot for 300 drivers
options.feedback: A paid pilot is better than praise, but the buyer signed, not the drivers. Until they keep using it after the pilot, it can still be a **false sign**.

options.text: That distributor's CEO praised the app on stage at an industry event
options.feedback: Public praise costs nothing and changes no routine. It's attention, a textbook **false sign of fit**.

options.text: Twelve small hauliers use it on almost every delivery and call within an hour when it goes down
options.feedback: Steady daily use plus panic when it breaks is **retention** in its clearest form. These customers have built their work around it.

cards.softwareNote: In business software, the buyer and the daily user are often different people. Check retention among the users, not just the contract renewals.

cards.title: Fit shows up in who stays, not who arrives.
body: You used two ideas: **retention as the real signal** (a curve that flattens) and **false signs of fit** (downloads, press, praise and pilots that measure attention).
**Try it today:** pick the customers who first bought from you two months ago. How many came back last week?
